---
title: "Change of Variables"
---



## The One Formula

Everything in this chapter rests on a single rule for how a probability density
changes when you push it through an invertible map.  It relates the density in the
data world to the density in the simple (Gaussian) world through one correction
factor — the Jacobian determinant — and it is what lets us move between the two
worlds without losing or inventing any probability.

If $z = T(x)$ is an **invertible** map and $z$ has density $p_Z$, then $x$ has
density

$$
p_X(x) = p_Z\big(T(x)\big)\,\left|\det \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|.
$$

The Jacobian determinant is a *volume* correction: it accounts for how much $T$
stretches or squeezes space at $x$.  This single equation is the engine of the
course.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What the Two Directions Mean

- **Forward** ($z = T(x)$, Gaussianize): the Jacobian tells you how much $T$ had
  to distort space to make $x$ look standard-normal — and that distortion *is* the
  dependence (made precise as [total correlation](03-mutual-information.qmd)).
- **Backward** ($x = T^{-1}(z)$): the formula is a sampling recipe — draw
  $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ and apply $T^{-1}$ to get a sample of $x$.  This is
  the generative direction used in [Uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd).
:::

## The 1-D Building Block: Rank → Gaussian

The simplest non-trivial $T$ makes a *single* variable Gaussian.  Send each value
through its own empirical CDF $\hat F$ (which maps any distribution to a uniform),
then through the inverse Gaussian CDF $\Phi^{-1}$:

$$
T(x) = \Phi^{-1}\big(\hat F(x)\big).
$$

This is monotone, hence invertible, so it carries no information away — it only
*reshapes the marginal*.  Cross-dependence between variables is untouched (that is
what [rotation](02-rbig.qmd) is for).

::: {#cell-fig-gaussianize-1d .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.exponential(size=4000)
g = gaussianize_1d(v)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
axL.hist(v, bins=40, color=WARM, alpha=0.8, density=True)
axL.set_title("before:  heavy-skewed", fontsize=12)
axL.set_xlabel("x"); axL.set_ylabel("density")
despine(axL)

grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 200)
axR.hist(g, bins=40, color=COOL, alpha=0.8, density=True)
axR.plot(grid, norm.pdf(grid), c=INK, lw=2, label="standard normal")
axR.set_title("after:  T(x) = Φ⁻¹(F̂(x))", fontsize=12)
axR.set_xlabel("z"); axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A skewed (exponential) variable, before and after the rank → Gaussian transform. The shape becomes a standard normal; the ordering of points is preserved.](01-change-of-variables_files/figure-html/fig-gaussianize-1d-output-1.png){#fig-gaussianize-1d width=1304 height=465}
:::
:::


## Why Invertibility Is the Whole Point

A lossy transform (say, thresholding) cannot be undone, so you can never get back
to the data — no sampling, no exact likelihood.  An *invertible* $T$ keeps a
perfect dictionary between the two worlds.  Anything easy in Gaussian space
(independent coordinates, closed-form densities) can be pulled back to the data
exactly.

::: {#cell-fig-monotone-map .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
order = np.argsort(v)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
ax.plot(v[order], g[order], c=COOL, lw=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel("x  (data value)"); ax.set_ylabel("z = T(x)  (Gaussian value)")
ax.set_title("A monotone, invertible relabelling", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(ax, 0.5, -0.12, "rank preserved  ⇒  no information lost")
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The 1-D map is monotone: it relabels the axis without reordering points, so it is exactly invertible.](01-change-of-variables_files/figure-html/fig-monotone-map-output-1.png){#fig-monotone-map width=764 height=464}
:::
:::


::: {.eli5}
**One-liner.**  Change of variables is a currency exchange between probability
worlds; the Jacobian is the exchange rate.  Make the rate invertible and you can
always convert back.
:::
